<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23220v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2507.23220-mechanistic-etm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-624e698062a65845">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:proeval" data-paper-title="ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-proeval-344b21b9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b5a18b39b2bf1adc">Why reuse historical per-item scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aproeval">ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cross-model correlations form a probabilistic surrogate, updated after limited queries to estimate total score and uncertainty. Estimates are not full evaluations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Query several items and predict the rest while reporting posterior variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23099">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.23099-proeval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b5a18b39b2bf1adc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:proeval" data-paper-title="ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b22fb32d4dcf178a">Why select a query before reading target scores and exclude the target from history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aproeval">ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Historical correlations supply a prior. Only actively selected responses update the posterior. An entire target column in covariance or selection leaks unqueried answers. Variance reduction does not guarantee robustness beyond historical distribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Select the most informative item first and query its score, rather than preload the target&#x27;s full column.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23099">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.23099-proeval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b22fb32d4dcf178a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:proeval" data-paper-title="ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-abfb841936daff0f">How does Bayesian quadrature acquisition differ from choosing the lowest current mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aproeval">ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>BQ maximizes expected reduction of overall wᵀKw variance, not difficulty. Failure-oriented acquisition has separate candidate conditions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An easy item correlated with many unqueried items can reduce score uncertainty substantially.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23099">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.23099-proeval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-abfb841936daff0f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:proeval" data-paper-title="ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9ddb161d95e906b1">Why reject duplicate target observations and target IDs in history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aproeval">ProEval: Proactive Failure Discovery and Efficient Performance Estimation for Generative AI Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Duplicates distort query budget and posterior updates; historical target scores leak unqueried outcomes into the prior. Only selected feedback is allowed. Three history records are a local minimum, not a theorem guarantee.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A target column already present in history invalidates claimed savings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 代码映射与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23099">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.23099-proeval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9ddb161d95e906b1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-tcab-036a095f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0b3ed7d3bbc398fd">Why share real feedback across adaptive policies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate A/B/n runs may pay repeatedly for identical context/action pairs. Coupling permits valid reuse while preserving each policy&#x27;s marginal trajectory distribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two policies choose the same action in the same state, one feedback can update both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0b3ed7d3bbc398fd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-31a085596f880eba">Why match full context and action before sharing TCAB feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Identical actions can yield different outcomes under different contexts. Tree maximal coupling matches complete pairs to share conditional rewards while preserving each policy&#x27;s marginal trajectory. Coupled policies are deliberately correlated, and savings do not prove global optimality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Picking the same product for different users does not justify sharing one click observation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31a085596f880eba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6c5e5b73ef108829">Does correlated coupling alter each policy&#x27;s own trajectory distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not necessarily. It changes joint dependence while preserving individual marginals. Equal final accuracy alone does not verify adaptive updates or marginal trajectory parity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two draws can coincide more frequently while each retains its original probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6c5e5b73ef108829">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-35f6f43d12979124">Why not count identical action strings as saved feedback calls?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reuse depends on full context and state conditions. The same action in different environments can yield different feedback. Compare actual shared queries and tree-edge differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two different users choosing A do not yield the same reusable observation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-35f6f43d12979124">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:xlgobench" data-paper-title="XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-xlgobench-677fa08c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e970d2cec3e9d35d">Why use tasks with deterministic algorithmic answers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Axlgobench">XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Controlled difficulty and exact answers reduce open-ended judging ambiguity. Compare real models across validated language versions; a scorer alone is not capability evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A state transition can use the same exact solver after changing its language.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30788v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2605.30788-xlgobench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e970d2cec3e9d35d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:xlgobench" data-paper-title="XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-40641ea146f76b91">Why don&#x27;t correct local algorithm answers establish cross-lingual gaps?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Axlgobench">XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exact scoring removes judge subjectivity, but validated translations and real model outputs across complexities are needed. Local generation has limited structure, not the full noise/difficulty matrix. Gold stays in the scorer, and five task diagnostics do not measure language accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An internal shortest-path solver can answer a graph, without testing whether two natural-language versions are equivalent or equally solvable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30788v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2605.30788-xlgobench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-40641ea146f76b91">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:xlgobench" data-paper-title="XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-daca851c3385f112">Is scorer correctness evidence of multilingual generalization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Axlgobench">XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It validates evaluation of a supplied prediction. Generalization needs real inputs and outputs across languages, complexity scans, and statistics. Small examples do not substitute for seven languages or human translation checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Solving a 12-node shortest path internally does not show an LM can answer it in a specific language.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30788v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2605.30788-xlgobench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-daca851c3385f112">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:xlgobench" data-paper-title="XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c3c5ef680fb6a56">Why does Pr-DSA top-eight scoring ignore order but reject duplicates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Axlgobench">XLGoBench: Detecting cross-lingual skill gaps with algorithmic tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The target is the complete eight-state set after full probability propagation. Reordering is harmless; repeats hide missing states. Other tasks also use full JSON matching, not partial credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Eight list entries beginning A,A,B may contain fewer than eight distinct states and must be rejected.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30788v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2605.30788-xlgobench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c3c5ef680fb6a56">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rosetta-unification" data-paper-title="Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-rosetta-unification-42d28816" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e283ba490c9106d0">Why can perfect same-language recall coexist with failed transfer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arosetta-unification">Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Language features can support separate knowledge representations. A fact readable in its training language need not be accessible in another. Controlled training isolates this distinction; ID scores cannot replace cross-language validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A birthplace appears only in language A: A paraphrases can all succeed while language B queries fail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11017v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2508.11017-rosetta-unification/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e283ba490c9106d0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rosetta-unification" data-paper-title="Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8230e66a99e4d014">Why is an explicit same-language baseline essential?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arosetta-unification">Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The score compares cross-language group similarity with a same-language baseline and averages ratios. Self-cosine fixed at one changes the definition. Local inputs explicitly identify groups/baselines and reject unstable denominators.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ratios 0.8/0.6 and 0.6/0.8 must be averaged; the ratio of their summed numerators and denominators is different.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11017v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2508.11017-rosetta-unification/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8230e66a99e4d014">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rosetta-unification" data-paper-title="Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ccd798e2e8e68a79">How does Rosetta differ from Thinking to Recall?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arosetta-unification">Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rosetta studies pretraining language distributions and representation unification; Thinking to Recall analyzes generated reasoning facts and their correctness. Similarity is not a truth judge, and oracle-conditioned accuracy does not establish multilingual unification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>More similar language representations do not verify a generated birthday; verified reasoning facts do not ensure low-resource-language access.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11017v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2508.11017-rosetta-unification/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ccd798e2e8e68a79">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rosetta-unification" data-paper-title="Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-91f883c07674fabc">Do passing arithmetic tests reproduce the reported 0.97 correlation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arosetta-unification">Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. That coefficient needs representations and independent accuracies from many trained models. Local arrays establish arithmetic only, without feature extraction or answers; any new selection experiment must use validation rather than test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A finite random-matrix ratio is not evidence from 110 training runs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11017v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2508.11017-rosetta-unification/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-91f883c07674fabc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:thinking-to-recall" data-paper-title="Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-thinking-to-recall-75a6061f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1f1300a5c5f8f35d">Why might thinking help a single-hop factual question?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Athinking-to-recall">Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The paper distinguishes extra-token computational buffering from factual priming. Both may aid knowledge readout, without making every thought correct or establishing that longer is always better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Dummy traces probe content-independent computation; related facts probe semantic priming.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09906v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.09906-thinking-to-recall/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1f1300a5c5f8f35d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:thinking-to-recall" data-paper-title="Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bcaa798381c505d2">Why must all trace conditions share the retained-question set?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Athinking-to-recall">Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dropping difficult questions only from the clean condition confounds filtering with question difficulty. With 100 samples per question, any empty condition excludes that question from every arm, followed by macro averaging.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A question with one clean trace and one with ninety still contribute equal question-level weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09906v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.09906-thinking-to-recall/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bcaa798381c505d2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:thinking-to-recall" data-paper-title="Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-26c83fa9c9887b9d">Can the clean-fact condition be deployed as an agent policy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Athinking-to-recall">Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not by this component. It uses post-hoc truth annotations to estimate offline conditional expectations. Deployment needs an oracle-free verifier with measured errors and costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Choosing a trace by gold correctness and feeding it to an actor leaks the answer rather than improving reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09906v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.09906-thinking-to-recall/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-26c83fa9c9887b9d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:thinking-to-recall" data-paper-title="Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6416371045655a44">Why does the API return summaries rather than the best trace?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Athinking-to-recall">Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It confines truth labels to an independent evaluator instead of exposing an oracle to actors or training selection. Retention counts and offline status are explicit; missing conditions are never fabricated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If no question has factual traces, the evaluator fails rather than reporting clean accuracy one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09906v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.09906-thinking-to-recall/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6416371045655a44">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:latent-generalization" data-paper-title="Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-latent-generalization-265f2cc5" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e016f2e859cc84f9">How does latent generalization differ from recalling exposed answers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alatent-generalization">Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It requires relations or combinations not explicitly exposed as completions. Exposed and held-out recall are separated because overall F1 can be dominated by seen answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With all={A,B,C} and heldout={C}, answering A and B yields exposed recall one and held-out recall zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01430v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.01430-latent-generalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e016f2e859cc84f9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:latent-generalization" data-paper-title="Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-059b3a359c603bf0">Does held-out recall one imply exact-set success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alatent-generalization">Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Exact matching requires the complete valid answer set with neither omissions nor false additions. Primary inclusion only checks one designated held-out answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predicting A,B,C plus false D recalls C perfectly but fails exact matching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01430v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.01430-latent-generalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-059b3a359c603bf0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:latent-generalization" data-paper-title="Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-27c6bab8250f947e">What differs from Thinking to Recall?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alatent-generalization">Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Latent generalization uses controlled acquisition/structure splits to test implicit completions; Thinking to Recall studies access to existing factual knowledge. Neither permits gold-conditioned teachers or post-hoc truth labels to leak to the deployed actor.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Better recall of one fact does not establish generalization to an unseen reversal relation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01430v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.01430-latent-generalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-27c6bab8250f947e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:latent-generalization" data-paper-title="Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-79f71e514d5d6dde">Why implement metrics instead of a simplified Gemini trainer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alatent-generalization">Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The study depends on private Gemini SFT, teacher traces and RL interfaces. Exact metrics are affordable and useful; inventing a generic RL loop would hide defining dependencies. Full training is explicitly not reproduced.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Random answer-set fixtures verify formulas, not Gemini&#x27;s out-of-distribution performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01430v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.01430-latent-generalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-79f71e514d5d6dde">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llm-stochasticity" data-paper-title="The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-llm-stochasticity-133d0a6f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8335bb71e04411d5">Why can a perfectly uniform histogram be nonrandom?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allm-stochasticity">The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Histograms describe marginal frequencies, not order. A deterministic 0,1,2,3 cycle is uniform while the next value is predictable; temporal checks are separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 1,024-element cycle has zero chi-square and still never repeats adjacent symbols.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06543v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.06543-llm-stochasticity/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8335bb71e04411d5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llm-stochasticity" data-paper-title="The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-83fe38b1f38d842f">How should a KS/chi-square p-value above 0.05 be interpreted?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allm-stochasticity">The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is non-rejection under specified assumptions, not a 95% probability of randomness or proof of independence. Selecting the best p-value after many prompts changes inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A crafted uniform cycle can obtain p=1 without supplying entropy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06543v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.06543-llm-stochasticity/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-83fe38b1f38d842f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llm-stochasticity" data-paper-title="The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b2fbd708dbb1b403">How does an external PRNG differ from randomness in stochastic rounding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allm-stochasticity">The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>This paper evaluates model-requested sampling, while a PRNG supplies a different controlled source. SR uses an explicit generator for adjacent-rounding probabilities and conditional means, not LLM randomness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>NumPy draws are not Gemini samples; SR generator tests establish no independence of natural-language outputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06543v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.06543-llm-stochasticity/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b2fbd708dbb1b403">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llm-stochasticity" data-paper-title="The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-eeba2316ffba1af7">Why not discard invalid values or missing samples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allm-stochasticity">The Illusion of Stochasticity in LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Discarding changes the evaluated distribution and count, potentially selecting favorable outputs. The API checks count, support and finiteness; parsing failures need separate reporting.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One thousand valid values plus twenty-four invalid ones are not a complete successful 1,024-sample run.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心机制与公式, 原文结果与限制, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06543v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.06543-llm-stochasticity/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eeba2316ffba1af7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:qe-length-normalization" data-paper-title="Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-qe-length-normalization-fae0f407" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8afab47abd83b7e9">Why is comparing arbitrary long and short translations insufficient to establish QE length bias?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aqe-length-normalization">Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quality, domain and difficulty may differ. The paper concatenates consecutive gold segments from one document and varies prefix length, controlling assumed error-free quality and domain before measuring score drift. This still depends on the gold translations being approximately error-free.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: a score drop after concatenating correct paragraphs of one article is a different control from comparing an easy advertisement with a difficult legal document.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22028v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2510.22028-qe-length-normalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8afab47abd83b7e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:qe-length-normalization" data-paper-title="Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-499312e689768aec">Does dividing an existing MetricX score by length reproduce training-time normalization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aqe-length-normalization">Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The source changes labels to R/|h|, trains a density predictor, and multiplies its output by the matching length. Post-processing a frozen model does not change its training distribution. The local core transforms targets and restores outputs without claiming a debiased model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: rating−5 gives targets−0.5 and−0.25 for lengths10 and20. Restoring both yields−5, but this identity does not establish learned density prediction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22028v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2510.22028-qe-length-normalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-499312e689768aec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:qe-length-normalization" data-paper-title="Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ab022e08119760af">Does density-target training solve the same problem as validation-fitted temperature scaling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aqe-length-normalization">Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Density training changes the relationship between supervision and length. Temperature scaling changes the sharpness of existing classification probabilities, generally without changing the predicted class. Neither substitutes for the other&#x27;s model and data requirements.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: dividing binary logits by2 softens confidence but does not train a translation-error score per unit length.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22028v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2510.22028-qe-length-normalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ab022e08119760af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:qe-length-normalization" data-paper-title="Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d2fbee47169ed6a">Why must the500-token group filter use tokenized concatenated prefixes rather than sums of independent segments?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aqe-length-normalization">Penalizing Length: Uncovering Systematic Bias in Quality Estimation Metrics</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tokenization depends on boundaries. The interface requires actual counts for the five concatenated prefixes and rejects the whole group if the fifth exceeds500. Keeping a partial group changes the matched control. Density training and restoration must also use one length unit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: five separately counted100-token segments need not concatenate to exactly500. If the fifth prefix measures501, all five are rejected.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22028v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2510.22028-qe-length-normalization/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8d2fbee47169ed6a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cultural-cue" data-paper-title="Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-cultural-cue-701f9550" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a4c318f71d636fc">Why does CuE intervene on latent cultural features rather than only adding a country prompt?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acultural-cue">Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It distinguishes missing knowledge from failed elicitation and constructs a white-box intervention using SAE features. Prompts and feature steering can complement each other. A country prototype is only a group proxy, not every individual&#x27;s culture.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: a model may know a rare regional dish yet always suggest common dishes without a location. Steering tests elicitation of represented knowledge, not cultural safety.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23301v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.23301-cultural-cue/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a4c318f71d636fc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cultural-cue" data-paper-title="Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-957214d86e09fec1">Does rho=0.1 mean retaining10% of SAE features?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acultural-cue">Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Section2.3 retains the smallest descending-MI set whose cumulative information reaches10% of total MI. Concentrated information can require very few features. A fixed feature-count fraction changes the method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: MI values0.97,0.01,0.01,0.01 require only the first feature at rho0.5, not half the dimensions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23301v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.23301-cultural-cue/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-957214d86e09fec1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cultural-cue" data-paper-title="Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e841df37bb0cb2cb">Why are CuE and DetectorScope different despite both max-pooling SAE features?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acultural-cue">Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pooling is only a shared representation step. CuE selects feature-country information and constructs residual interventions from prototype differences. DetectorScope uses description-validation masks and a sparse detection head with attributions. A steering direction is not a detector and a head weight is not a cultural intervention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: a food feature may distinguish countries without distinguishing human from AI text. A large detection contribution does not establish culturally faithful generation when steering it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23301v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.23301-cultural-cue/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e841df37bb0cb2cb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cultural-cue" data-paper-title="Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9a96eaffcdc6fb16">Why average other country prototypes equally rather than pool all other examples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acultural-cue">Steering LLMs for Culturally Localized Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The formula compares the target prototype with the mean of other country prototypes, not a sample-count-weighted baseline. Pooling all assertions overweights countries with more examples. Decoder rows must also match the selected layer/features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: B has two values2 and C one value0. The other-country baseline is1, not4/3. A target value4 therefore yields difference3, not8/3.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23301v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.23301-cultural-cue/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9a96eaffcdc6fb16">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:decoding-constrained-beam" data-paper-title="Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-decoding-constrained-beam-7d0bad73" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-668c7dba6665932c">Why does a failed greedy verbatim match not imply zero near-verbatim extraction risk?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adecoding-constrained-beam">Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · AVERI / Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Greedy examines one locally preferred path. Multiple nearby variants can have substantial combined mass. CBS enumerates only a subset, so its sum is a deterministic lower bound rather than an unbiased estimate of all risk.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: two punctuation variants each have probability0.08. A different greedy path does not erase their known combined mass0.16.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24917v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.24917-decoding-constrained-beam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-668c7dba6665932c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:decoding-constrained-beam" data-paper-title="Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-853ada14e4653cef">Why normalize inside top-k and avoid pruning the final expansion back to B?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adecoding-constrained-beam">Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · AVERI / Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The audit targets the actual top-k decoding distribution, not the full softmax. Path probabilities use its conditionals. Final pruning would discard already enumerated valid mass, so the algorithm retains up toB×k finals. Surviving paths are not renormalized after beam pruning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: probabilities0.5,0.3,0.2 become0.625,0.375 under top2. Even with B1, both final expansions are retained.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24917v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.24917-decoding-constrained-beam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-853ada14e4653cef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:decoding-constrained-beam" data-paper-title="Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e5f81f1a027a0060">Can a CBS probability lower bound replace a DetectorScope AI-authorship score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adecoding-constrained-beam">Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · AVERI / Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. CBS uses a target suffix and model conditionals to bound near-target generation mass. DetectorScope predicts source from SAE text features. High generatability is not proof of authorship, and the statistics have different targets and labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: a common public sentence may have high model probability while being human-written. An authorship score likewise does not establish extraction probability for a training passage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24917v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.24917-decoding-constrained-beam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e5f81f1a027a0060">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:decoding-constrained-beam" data-paper-title="Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-84ee62e986a4b99f">Why check D[T,T] at the end even if the Levenshtein row minimum stays within epsilon?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adecoding-constrained-beam">Estimating near-verbatim extraction risk in language models with decoding-constrained beam search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · AVERI / Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The row minimum permits low-cost alignment to some target prefix, a necessary condition for intermediate viability. Final acceptance must compare the full target. Treating survival as success can count paths that do not match its end. Banked mass is only potential mass.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: closeness to prefix a does not establish closeness to full target abc. Exhaustive tests check LB≤p≤LB+bank and exact recovery with a wide beam.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24917v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2603.24917-decoding-constrained-beam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-84ee62e986a4b99f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:storyscope" data-paper-title="StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-storyscope-91aa94e5" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-409045ced6c7e999">How do StoryScope narrative features differ from counts of stereotypical AI words?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Astoryscope">StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · University of Maryland, College Park</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They describe discourse-level choices such as thematic explicitness, agency and temporal structure, derived through matched-prompt comparison and LLM feature discovery/assignment. Keyword counts do not execute that semantic pipeline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: two stories can use different vocabulary yet both explicitly state a moral at the end. The narrative choice is not one word&#x27;s presence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03136v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.03136-storyscope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-409045ced6c7e999">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:storyscope" data-paper-title="StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-de1fa713fe07f924">Why can the highest-SHAP feature still fail cross-model core selection?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Astoryscope">StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-13 · University of Maryland, College Park</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Core membership also requires stability, null significance, top25 frequency, a human–AI mean gap and limited spread across all five AI models. A source-specific signal can be a fingerprint rather than a core. The local gate is conjunctive, not a weighted score.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: five AI means0.8,0.8,0.8,0.8,0 have spread0.8, exceeding0.35 even if SHAP is maximal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03136v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2604.03136-storyscope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-de1fa713fe07f924">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
